principle_name: MEDDICC: A Deal Qualification Framework, Not a Sales Methodology
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: Apply MEDDICC to every deal from the first meeting onward—use it as a running qualification checklist that highlights what you know, what you don't know, and what your next move must be.
when_not_to_use: MEDDICC does not replace prospect-facing discovery methodology (SPIN, Gap Selling). It is a deal management framework that runs alongside and behind your customer conversations, not instead of them.
principle: MEDDICC is a systematic deal qualification framework designed to help salespeople evaluate, manage, and drive opportunities to close. The acronym stands for: Metrics, Economic Buyer, Decision Criteria, Decision Process, Identify Pain, Champion, Competitor. Each letter represents a component that must be understood and developed over the course of a sales cycle. MEDDICC highlights what has been achieved in a deal and reveals the gaps that determine the next required action. It enables consistent deal reviews, accurate forecasting, and disciplined qualification. It was developed at PTC in the 1990s by Dick Dunkel, adopted by John McMahon, and helped grow PTC from $300M to over $1B in revenue.
questions_to_ask: What do I know about each MEDDICC component for this deal?
Where are the gaps—which components have I not yet developed?
What is my specific plan to close each gap on the next call?
recommended_action: At every stage of every deal, review all seven MEDDICC components. Identify gaps. Build a specific action plan to address each gap before moving the deal to the next stage. Never present a proposal or close for commitment until all seven components are at least partially understood.
motm_application: MOTM BD reps and Sales Engineers should run every active opportunity through MEDDICC before each call or proposal. It instantly reveals whether a deal is genuinely qualified or simply 'felt good.' For MOTM, the most commonly missing elements are: Metrics (pain not quantified), Economic Buyer (only talking to a champion, not the MD), and Decision Process (no clarity on how approval actually happens).

principle_name: Three Levels of Pain: Technical, Business, and Personal
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: In every discovery conversation—push systematically through all three levels of pain before presenting any solution or proposal.
when_not_to_use: Do not attempt to uncover personal pain too early in the relationship—build trust through technical and business pain questions first.
principle: There are three levels of pain, each progressively more powerful as a driver of action. Technical pain is the surface symptom—missed deadlines, operational inefficiencies, inconsistent reporting. It is rarely enough to compel a decision. Business pain is the commercial impact of the technical pain—lost revenue, reduced profitability, inaccurate forecasting that prevents hiring decisions. It can push a prospect toward action. Personal pain is the emotional and individual consequence—the MD's stressful board meetings, the VP's fear for their job, the manager's frustration explaining the same problem repeatedly. Personal pain is the emotional decision-making driver—it is what makes people urgently want to solve problems, not just acknowledge them.
questions_to_ask: What operational challenges is this creating for your team right now? (Technical)
How does this affect your revenue, margin, or ability to hit targets? (Business)
What does it mean for you personally when this comes up in management meetings? (Personal)
If this isn't solved in six months, what does that look like for the business—and for you?
recommended_action: In every discovery conversation, do not stop at technical pain. Ask follow-up questions that move from surface symptoms to business impact to personal consequences. Only when all three levels are uncovered—and ideally quantified—is the pain fully developed.
motm_application: In MOTM discovery: Technical pain = 'our sales reps don't update the CRM consistently.' Business pain = 'our pipeline is unpredictable and our revenue forecast last quarter was off by 30%.' Personal pain = 'I'm having increasingly difficult conversations with my board about growth targets I can't confidently predict.' MOTM should not pitch until all three levels are confirmed. Personal pain is what makes the MD urgently want to act—not just nod along.

principle_name: Situational and Pain Questions: The Discovery Sequence
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: In every discovery conversation—always lead with 2–4 situational questions before asking pain questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not jump directly to pain questions without situational context—it feels abrupt and presumptuous. Build the context first.
principle: Effective discovery follows a deliberate two-phase sequence. First, situational questions establish context and open the conversation: mirroring (repeating a phrase back), TED questions ('Tell me, describe to me, explain to me'), and deliberate silence after short answers. These are lower-risk and build rapport. Second, pain questions move the conversation from symptoms to impact: labeling ('Sounds like this is also a data challenge'), impact questions ('How does that affect the business?'), and current/future state questions ('What happens if we're speaking in three months and this hasn't changed?'). Ask 2–4 situational questions before introducing a pain question. This ratio ensures context is established before you probe for depth.
questions_to_ask: Tell me more about that—describe what happens when that breaks down. (TED)
[Mirror] Tricky forecast meetings? [Silence]
Sounds like this is both an operational and a credibility issue. (Label)
Help me understand how this impacts the business. (Impact)
What happens if you don't solve this now—or in the next six months? (Future state)
recommended_action: Prepare 2–4 situational discovery questions before every meeting. Use mirroring and TED questions to keep the prospect talking. When a short answer comes, use silence—don't fill it. Use labeling and impact questions once context is established to move from technical to business and personal pain.
motm_application: MOTM first meeting sequence: (Situational) 'Tell me about your current sales team structure and how territory is managed.' [Mirror any interesting response.] (TED) 'Explain to me what a typical week looks like for a rep in terms of prospecting activity.' [Silence after short answers.] (Pain) 'Sounds like the consistency of activity is a challenge—how does that affect your ability to forecast?' [Impact] 'Help me understand what unpredictable forecasting means for the business this year.' This sequence surfaces the pain that makes MOTM's solution relevant.

principle_name: Uncovering Personal Pain Without Being Intrusive
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: After business pain has been established and the relationship has enough trust for a deeper conversation—use one of the four techniques to surface personal implications.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask direct personal questions too early or in a group setting where the prospect may feel exposed. Use detachment and labeling in group contexts; empathy and permission in more private, one-on-one conversations.
principle: Personal pain is the emotional driver that separates deals that close urgently from those that stall indefinitely. However, asking 'How does this affect you personally?' can feel too direct and intrusive. Four techniques allow personal pain to surface naturally: (1) Detachment—change the subject from 'you' to a third-party noun ('What would that conversation look like with your CEO?'); (2) Labeling—name the emotional dimension neutrally ('Feels like you'll need to have a tough conversation with your board if this continues'); (3) Empathy—use a sensitive tone ('It feels like you're personally invested in solving this—talk to me about that'); (4) Permission—pre-frame the question ('Can I ask you a tough question?') to lower the prospect's guard before probing.
questions_to_ask: What would that conversation look like with your board if nothing changes? (Detachment)
Feels like you're going to have to have a difficult conversation with your MD if this isn't fixed soon. (Labeling)
It feels like you're personally invested in this—tell me more about that. (Empathy)
Can I ask you a tough question? (Permission)
recommended_action: After uncovering business pain, choose the appropriate technique based on the relationship and setting. In a first meeting or group context, use detachment or labeling. In a second meeting or one-on-one, empathy and permission become available. Always follow the technique with silence—let the prospect go where they want to go.
motm_application: After MOTM has confirmed that an MD's pipeline is unpredictable: 'If you're still in the same position six months from now, what does that conversation with your board look like?' (Detachment). This invites the MD to describe the personal consequence—a difficult board meeting, a question about competence, a growth target missed—without MOTM making it uncomfortably direct. That response is the personal pain that makes urgency real.

principle_name: Metrics: Quantify Every Pain to Make It Real and Defensible
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: At every stage where a pain or problem has been identified—immediately attempt to quantify it in numbers. There is no scenario where uncovering metrics harms a deal.
when_not_to_use: Never fabricate or estimate metrics for the prospect—ask them to provide the numbers. If they don't have them, make it a homework item: 'Can you come back to me with that number by Thursday?'
principle: Metrics are the quantifiable outcomes the prospect is seeking—and the numbers that make their current pain tangible and serious. Quantifying pain serves four purposes: (1) it minimizes the perceived cost of the solution relative to the size of the problem; (2) it illustrates and compounds the scale of the issue ('if each lost deal is worth ₹5L and you're losing 10 per month, that's ₹50L per month'); (3) it forces the prospect to conduct internal investigation, which increases organizational investment in solving the problem; (4) numbers are memorable and repeatable—the prospect can use them to build the internal business case without you being present. Ask for the metrics. Take them away and build the ROI case offline.
questions_to_ask: What does that cost you per month in lost revenue or productivity?
How much of your team's time is going into working around this problem?
If you could quantify the impact of this problem, what number would you put on it?
How many customers or deals have you lost because of this in the last six months?
What would a 10% improvement in this area mean for your revenue this year?
recommended_action: After every pain statement from the prospect, immediately follow with a quantification question. Build a running list of metrics across the discovery conversation. Before any proposal, translate each pain into a specific number that the prospect has confirmed. Use these numbers in the proposal to anchor the value of the solution against the cost of the problem.
motm_application: When an MOTM prospect says 'our sales reps don't follow up consistently,' ask: 'How many meetings per week do your reps conduct, and what percentage do you estimate don't get a proper follow-up?' Then: 'If we assume 20 meetings per week with 40% inconsistent follow-up, that's 8 missed opportunities per week. What is an average deal worth for you?' The number that emerges—₹40L per month in at-risk pipeline—makes MOTM's engagement fee look very different than if the pain had been left unquantified.

principle_name: Economic Buyer: Identify and Engage the Person with Real Authority
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: As early as possible in any opportunity—identify who holds budget authority and final decision-making power. Every deal requires direct engagement with the Economic Buyer before a proposal is submitted.
when_not_to_use: Do not confuse a well-informed champion with an Economic Buyer—they are always different people. A champion can have influence; only the Economic Buyer has authority.
principle: The Economic Buyer is the individual who holds both the budget and the authority to make the final purchasing decision. Without their engagement, even the most advanced deal can collapse at the last step when someone who has not been involved in the process overrides or delays it. MEDDICC requires that the Economic Buyer is identified, engaged, and has agreed to specific next steps. The Economic Buyer must always be a different person from the Champion—one has influence, the other has authority. If you are only meeting with the Champion, you are not yet in front of the person who can actually sign.
questions_to_ask: Who ultimately makes the final decision on investments like this?
If we were to move to a proposal, who would need to sign off on it?
Is there a budget owner who would need to be involved in approving this?
Along with yourself, who else really cares about solving this problem?
recommended_action: In every deal, explicitly identify the Economic Buyer by name and title. Confirm that you have direct access to them, or a specific plan to get it. Do not submit a proposal to a Champion and expect them to sell it upward—build a strategy to get the Economic Buyer into at least one conversation before or during the proposal stage.
motm_application: In most MOTM deals, the initial contact is a Sales Manager or VP Sales (the Champion). The Economic Buyer is almost always the MD or CEO who controls the budget. MOTM should never submit a proposal to the Sales Manager alone. The goal is always to get in front of the MD—either directly or through the Champion who uses Need-payoff Questions to build their internal case. Without the MD engaged, no MOTM deal is truly qualified.

principle_name: Champion: Build and Enable an Internal Advocate
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: As early as possible in any deal—identify who within the prospect's organization has influence, is motivated to support your solution, and can sell on your behalf when you are not in the room.
when_not_to_use: Do not confuse a coach (who gives you insight but has no influence) with a Champion. A coach is useful for information; only a Champion can drive internal change. Do not assume someone is a Champion because they are friendly—test their willingness to advocate actively.
principle: The Champion is an internal advocate within the prospect's organization who believes in your solution and actively works to drive it through the buying process. A Champion has real influence over the Economic Buyer and other stakeholders. They validate your solution internally when you are not present, build the internal case, and create momentum you cannot create yourself. A Coach, by contrast, has useful information but no influence—they are helpful for intelligence but cannot drive decisions. Effective deals require at least one Champion; strong deals have Champions at multiple levels and functions. Your job is to identify, develop, and equip the Champion to sell for you internally.
questions_to_ask: Who in your organization is most motivated to solve this problem?
Who would most benefit from getting this right?
Are you able to bring this to your MD/leadership team, and how would you frame it?
What information would help you make the strongest possible case internally?
recommended_action: Identify your Champion by asking who is most personally invested in solving the problem (personal pain). Test their willingness to advocate by asking them to set up a meeting with the Economic Buyer, share materials internally, or take a next step on your behalf. Equip them with quantified pain metrics and clear business case framing so they can sell effectively without you. A Champion who cannot or will not make introductions upward is probably a Coach, not a Champion.
motm_application: In MOTM deals, the Sales Manager or VP Sales is typically the Champion. MOTM's job is to equip them to sell the MOTM concept to their MD. Use Need-payoff Questions in the Champion conversation to get them articulating the value in their own words—the same words they'll use in their MD conversation. Then test champion strength: 'Would you be comfortable setting up a 30-minute call with your MD so we can discuss the business case together?' A yes = Champion. A maybe or hesitation = Coach.

principle_name: Multi-threading: Eliminate Single Points of Failure
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: From the first meeting onward—map all relevant stakeholders and build relationships across multiple functions and levels simultaneously. Never allow a deal to depend on a single contact.
when_not_to_use: Do not go over a contact's head without either their knowledge or a very specific strategic reason. Multi-thread with respect for existing relationships, not in circumvention of them.
principle: Multi-threading means engaging multiple stakeholders across different levels and functions within a prospect's organization simultaneously. Deals that depend on a single contact—one champion, one gatekeeper—are fragile. If that person leaves, gets sick, changes priorities, or loses internal influence, the deal collapses. Multi-threading eliminates this risk by distributing the deal relationship across multiple stakeholders. Additional benefits: stakeholders validate your solution to each other when you are not present; the dynamics of their relationships can work in your favor (making one look good in front of another); and people are more likely to commit when they have done so in front of colleagues. MEDDICC's structure forces multi-threading by requiring both an Economic Buyer and a Champion to be identified and engaged—as two different people.
questions_to_ask: Who else in your organization is affected by this challenge?
Along with yourself, who else really cares about getting this right?
Who in your leadership team would find the ROI case most relevant?
Who else should be part of this conversation to make sure we get it right?
recommended_action: In every deal, map out all relevant stakeholders using a 3x3 matrix: three levels (Economic Buyer, Champion, Coach/User) across three functions (your ICP function plus two adjacent functions). Build a specific plan to engage each relevant stakeholder. Use the Economic Buyer's strategic priorities as justification for requesting introductions to other stakeholders.
motm_application: For a typical MOTM deal with a manufacturing company, the 3x3 matrix might look like: Economic Buyer = MD (Sales function), VP Operations (adjacent), CFO (adjacent). Champion = VP Sales, Head of Production Planning, Financial Controller. A deal that is only threaded through the VP Sales is vulnerable. MOTM should plan to reach the MD directly and, where relevant, involve the CFO in the ROI conversation. Each stakeholder validates the MOTM decision to the others.

principle_name: The 3x3 Stakeholder Matrix: Map Every Relevant Contact
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: At the beginning of every qualified opportunity—before second meetings and before any proposal is submitted.
when_not_to_use: Do not create a 3x3 matrix for transactional or very short sales cycles where a single decision maker exists. This is for complex, multi-stakeholder deals.
principle: The 3x3 stakeholder matrix is a tool for systematically mapping all relevant stakeholders across three levels (Economic Buyer, Champion, Coach/User) and three functions (your primary ICP function plus two adjacent functions whose stakeholders are affected by the problem or decision). For example, if selling to a Sales VP, adjacent functions might be RevOps and Marketing. The matrix surfaces who you should be speaking with but are not yet, reveals the relevant stakeholders at each level, and enables a prioritized engagement plan. Every cell in the matrix represents a potential relationship to build and a risk eliminated.
recommended_action: For every qualified deal, draw the 3x3 matrix explicitly: list the three relevant functions across the top, and the three stakeholder levels down the side. Fill in the specific principle_names and titles for each cell. Identify which cells are currently blank (not yet engaged). Build a specific plan to engage the most critical missing stakeholders—starting with the Economic Buyer if not yet reached.
motm_application: MOTM 3x3 example for a mid-size manufacturing company: Functions = Sales, Operations, Finance. Economic Buyer row = MD (Sales), VP Operations, CFO. Champion row = VP Sales, Head of Procurement or Production, Financial Controller. Coach/User row = Sales Manager, Ops Manager, Finance Analyst. MOTM's typical entry point is the VP Sales (Champion in Sales column). The most critical gaps are usually the MD (Economic Buyer) and the CFO (adjacent Economic Buyer). Plan specifically for how to reach those two.

principle_name: How to Get Introductions to New Stakeholders
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: After identifying gaps in the 3x3 matrix—when you need to escalate the conversation to a higher level or bring in a new function.
when_not_to_use: Never use the lazy question 'Is there anyone else we should invite to the next call?'—it is too easy to sidestep and signals that you don't know who the important stakeholders are.
principle: Getting introductions to stakeholders who are not yet engaged requires a structured approach. Three techniques work: (1) Use strategic priorities—connect the new stakeholder's known priorities to the problem being discussed, making the introduction feel necessary and logical ('We should bring in Sarah because this directly affects her drive to improve win rates'); (2) Reference-similar-success—use social proof from other deals to justify why a specific role should be involved ('Other companies I've worked with found that involving the CFO at this stage helped accelerate the ROI conversation significantly'); (3) Go direct—when appropriate, reach out to the unstated stakeholder directly, referencing the current conversation as context. Never ask generic multi-threading questions; always make the introduction request specific and logical.
questions_to_ask: At this point, we should bring [Name] into this conversation because [their strategic priority] is directly connected to what we're solving—what's their email?
Other organizations I've worked with found that involving [role] here had a significant impact on the decision. Would [Name] be relevant to invite?
I'd like to speak with [Name] directly to make sure the ROI case is fully aligned to [their specific concern]—could you make an introduction?
recommended_action: Before every meeting, identify the one stakeholder you most need to reach who is not yet engaged. Prepare a specific, logical reason tied to their known strategic priorities for why they should be involved. Use that reason to make the introduction request in the meeting or follow-up. Never ask a generic multi-threading question.
motm_application: MOTM rep in a call with the VP Sales: 'At this point, the business case we're building directly connects to the MD's priority of improving new account acquisition. I'd like to bring him into a 30-minute conversation to make sure the plan we build is aligned to his objectives. Would you be comfortable setting that up?' This is specific, logical, and gives the VP Sales a clear reason to facilitate—rather than a vague 'should we invite anyone else?'

principle_name: Decision Criteria: Understand, Shape, and Reframe How Evaluation Happens
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: As early as possible in any deal—identify the criteria the prospect is using to evaluate solutions, understand why each criterion matters, introduce criteria that favor your strengths, and position your solution accordingly.
when_not_to_use: Do not try to reshape decision criteria in an aggressive or transparent way that makes the prospect feel manipulated. Influence criteria through questions and stories, not by telling the prospect what they should care about.
principle: Decision Criteria are the specific factors a prospect uses to evaluate potential solutions—price, features, integration ease, ROI, scalability, support, adoption, etc. Most prospects have pre-defined criteria but have not thought deeply about all of them. Your job is three-fold: understand the root cause of each criterion (why does ease of use matter—what happened before?); introduce criteria that are missing but matter based on your competitive strengths; and position your solution as the best fit against those criteria. Transactional deals descend to price conversations because no other criteria have been established. The antidote is a rich, prospect-confirmed set of criteria that include dimensions where your solution excels.
questions_to_ask: What criteria are most important to you in evaluating a solution like this?
You mentioned ease of use is a priority—why is that particularly important for your team?
What's missing from your current shortlist of criteria? Have you thought about how you'll measure adoption after implementation?
How would it help if you had a solution that addressed not just X but also Y, which we've seen is critical for companies like yours?
recommended_action: In discovery, ask the prospect to share their top 3–5 evaluation criteria. For each one, probe the root cause ('why is that important?'). Then introduce 1–2 criteria that are missing but where you have a strong advantage, framed as a question or story rather than a pitch. Before submitting a proposal, confirm how the prospect is weighting or ranking each criterion—this directly reveals where to focus the proposal.
motm_application: MOTM prospect says criteria are: price, proven results, flexibility of engagement. MOTM should probe 'why price?' to understand if it's a budget constraint or confidence issue. Then introduce missing criteria: 'Most sales leaders we work with also care deeply about how quickly the engagement produces visible results—have you thought about how you'll measure impact at 60 days?' This introduces a timeline/accountability criterion where MOTM has a defined approach that many competitors do not.

principle_name: Decision Process: Map Both 'Getting to Yes' and the Paper Process
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: Once a qualified opportunity is established—map the full decision process in two phases: everything required to get to a 'yes,' and everything required after a 'yes' to actually execute the contract and begin.
when_not_to_use: Do not skip the paper process phase—legal, procurement, and contract steps are as important to map as the decision steps, and deals often stall between 'yes' and signature.
principle: The Decision Process consists of two separate and equally important phases. Phase 1: Getting to 'Yes'—all the steps, meetings, internal approvals, and stakeholders involved in the prospect committing to your solution. Phase 2: The Paper Process—all the legal, procurement, contract review, and administrative steps required to get from 'yes' to signed agreement and implementation. Most salespeople map Phase 1 adequately but ignore Phase 2, leading to unexpected delays and forecast inaccuracies after a verbal commitment. Understanding both phases gives accurate forecast timelines and prevents surprise obstacles. The Mutual Action Plan (MAP) should cover both phases explicitly.
questions_to_ask: Once you've made the decision internally, what are the steps between that decision and a signed agreement?
Is there a procurement or legal review process? Typically how long does that take?
Who else needs to be involved in the approval process beyond the people we've spoken with?
Have you been through a procurement process like this recently? What did that look like?
Are there any compliance, security, or legal reviews that would need to happen?
recommended_action: In every deal, map both phases explicitly. Ask the prospect to walk you through what happens after they say yes—who signs, who reviews the contract, what the procurement timeline looks like. Build this into the Mutual Action Plan with real dates and owners. Flag it during deal reviews as a qualification criterion: if you don't know the paper process, the deal is not fully qualified.
motm_application: MOTM deals often involve a relatively fast decision (MD says yes) followed by unexpected delays: 'Our CFO needs to review the engagement terms,' 'Our legal team has some questions about IP,' 'We need to raise a purchase order first.' MOTM should uncover these steps before committing a close date. Ask: 'Once we agree commercially, what does the process look like between that agreement and the actual start date?' Then map those steps into the Mutual Action Plan.

principle_name: The Mutual Action Plan: Build the Path to Outcome with the Prospect
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: Once a deal has been qualified to the point where a shared path forward can be built—typically after the first or second meeting, once pain and decision process are partially understood.
when_not_to_use: Do not create a MAP unilaterally and send it to the prospect to review—it must be built collaboratively to create shared ownership. A MAP imposed by the seller is just a close plan; a MAP built together creates genuine accountability.
principle: A Mutual Action Plan (MAP) is a prospect-facing document co-created with the prospect that outlines the actions, owners, and dates required to achieve the outcome the prospect has defined. Critically, it is not a close plan—it does not end with 'contract signature.' It ends with the outcome the prospect achieves after implementation. Building the MAP together creates accountability on both sides. Turn completed items green at each touchpoint to reinforce progress. The MAP is anchored to the Critical Event—a real, non-negotiable date in the prospect's calendar that they cannot afford to miss (board meeting, fiscal year end, new hire cohort, product launch). This is different from a compelling event created by the seller.
questions_to_ask: What date do you need this in place by, and what happens if that date slips?
What are the steps between now and that date that we need to work backward from?
Who on your side would own each of these actions?
Are there any internal reviews or approvals we should build into the timeline?
recommended_action: In the meeting where a deal becomes real, open a shared document or screenshare and build the MAP together in real time. Include every action, its owner, and its date. Identify the Critical Event at the end of the MAP and work backward from it. Share the MAP in every follow-up email. Update it on every call. Use it as the structure for all follow-up communications instead of 'just checking in' emails.
motm_application: MOTM MAP example: Date 05/10 – MD and VP Sales align on engagement scope (Owner: MD). Date 10/10 – MOTM sends commercial proposal (Owner: MOTM). Date 17/10 – CFO reviews commercials (Owner: CFO). Date 24/10 – Decision call (Owner: MD). Date 01/11 – Agreement signed (Owner: Both). Date 15/11 – Kickoff (Owner: Both). Date 01/02 – 90-day review (Owner: Both). The Critical Event: the company's Q1 planning cycle starts in January and the MD needs the MOTM engagement running before then to influence Q1 targets.

principle_name: Critical Event vs. Compelling Event: Anchor Urgency to Reality
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: When a deal lacks genuine urgency and you need to anchor the timeline to a real business consequence rather than a seller-manufactured deadline.
when_not_to_use: Never invent or exaggerate a Critical Event—if it is not real and discoverable, the prospect will dismiss it and it will damage trust. A Compelling Event (seller-created urgency like a discount deadline) has its place, but a Critical Event is always stronger.
principle: A Critical Event is a real, time-sensitive business milestone in the prospect's world that they cannot afford to miss—a board presentation, a fiscal year start, a new hire cohort, a product launch, a regulatory deadline. The Critical Event creates natural urgency because the consequence of missing it is real and entirely on the prospect's side. A Compelling Event, by contrast, is a deadline or incentive created by the seller—an end-of-month discount, a limited availability window. Compelling Events have some utility but are weaker than Critical Events because the prospect knows they are artificial. The MAP should always be anchored to a Critical Event. Uncovering the Critical Event often requires probing: 'What happens for the business if this isn't in place by X?'
questions_to_ask: Is there a date in your calendar by which you need this solved—a board review, a planning cycle, a new team cohort?
What happens for the business if this isn't in place by that date?
Is there any specific date that this decision really needs to be made by to avoid a knock-on consequence?
If we slip by two months, what does that cost you internally?
recommended_action: In every deal, explicitly seek the Critical Event. Ask the prospect what upcoming milestone makes this decision time-sensitive from their perspective. Build the MAP backward from that date. If no Critical Event surfaces, use the quantified pain metrics to create urgency around the cost of inaction (the ongoing monthly cost of not solving the problem becomes a de facto Critical Event).
motm_application: MOTM rep discovers that the MD's company begins annual sales target-setting in January and the board reviews sales productivity in Q1. The Critical Event = January planning cycle. MOTM frames all urgency around this: 'For the MOTM engagement to influence your Q1 targets, we'd need to be operational by December at the latest—which means a decision by the first week of November. Does that timeline work?' This is not artificial urgency—it is real business logic anchored to the prospect's calendar.

principle_name: Competitive Discovery: Ask What They Like Before What They Don't Like
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: Whenever a competitor is involved in the deal—ask about competitors using the same discovery sequence as pain discovery. Begin with what the prospect likes about the competitor.
when_not_to_use: Never launch into competitive positioning by immediately listing your advantages over the competitor—this triggers defensiveness and sounds like a sales pitch. Ask questions first.
principle: Competitive positioning requires preparation (battlecards) and discipline (ask before you pitch). When a competitor is identified, resist the urge to immediately explain why you are better. Instead, apply the same discovery sequence used for pain: (1) Ask what the prospect liked about the competitor's offer (this lowers resistance and shows confidence); (2) Ask what they didn't like or what concerned them (this surfaces doubts you can address); (3) Probe specifically into the competitor's known weaknesses using situational and pain questions; (4) Use stories (STAR method) to position your solution as the answer—with the customer as the hero, not you. The goal is to have the prospect articulate the reasons they are concerned about the competitor—then you don't have to argue it.
questions_to_ask: What did you like about Competitor X's offer?
What did you not like, or what raised a concern for you?
How important is [competitive weakness] to you?
Tell me more about that concern—how would that impact your team if it materialized?
What happens in six months if [competitive weakness] becomes a real problem?
recommended_action: Prepare battlecards for every competitor you encounter regularly. Before any competitive conversation, know: their strengths, your landmines (your weaknesses they will exploit), their weaknesses, and how you win. In the meeting, open with appreciation for the competitor, then probe concerns using discovery questions. Use a STAR story to let a reference customer explain why your solution was the right choice.
motm_application: If a MOTM prospect says they're considering a lower-cost sales training provider, MOTM should not immediately argue superiority. Ask: 'What did you find appealing about their approach?' Then: 'What concerns did you have about how they would work in your specific environment—industrial B2B with long OEM sales cycles?' Then probe the concern: 'If the training approach doesn't match how your buyers actually buy, what does that mean for adoption?' Let the prospect articulate the risk of the wrong choice. Then use a STAR story of a manufacturing client who went through that exact evaluation.

principle_name: STAR Stories for Competitive Positioning: Let the Customer Be the Hero
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: After competitive discovery has surfaced what the prospect values and fears in the competitive alternative—use a STAR story to position your solution without pitching directly.
when_not_to_use: Never tell a STAR story where your company is the hero—the customer or champion must be the central figure. Keep the company details minimal and use a relatable persona.
principle: The STAR storytelling method (Situation, Task/Pain, Action, Result) is the most effective way to position your solution competitively without pitching. The structure: (S) Situational context that mirrors the prospect's own situation—use a persona that closely matches them; (T) The pain and impact that person was experiencing—ideally the same pain you uncovered in discovery; (A) The action taken—how they evaluated options, what they chose, and what differentiated the winning solution; (R) The quantified result—a specific number they achieved. The key principle is that the customer is always the hero of the story, not the seller or the product. Stories bypass defensiveness because they don't feel like an argument.
recommended_action: For every product or service you sell, prepare 2–3 STAR stories covering your most common competitive scenarios. Match the story's persona closely to your prospect's profile. After delivering competitive discovery, segue naturally: 'That reminds me of Sarah, who runs a similar sales team at a manufacturing company...' Then deliver the full STAR story. End with the quantified result. Do not explicitly say 'and that's why you should choose us.'
motm_application: MOTM STAR story after competitive discovery: S = 'That reminds me of a VP Sales at a precision engineering company.' T = 'He had a real challenge with his reps generating meetings but not converting them—his pipeline was unpredictable and his MD was questioning whether the sales investment was paying off.' A = 'He'd looked at a couple of lower-cost training options but was concerned about their lack of industrial B2B context, so he brought MOTM in for a 90-day pilot.' R = 'In 90 days, his team went from generating 8 new OEM meetings per month to 23, and two of those converted to proposals in the first quarter.' The prospect is the hero, the result is specific, and MOTM never said 'that's why you should pick us.'

principle_name: The MEDDICC Checklist: Use It to Find and Close the Gaps
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: Before every deal review, before every proposal submission, before every forecast submission—run the full MEDDICC checklist and act on every 'no' answer.
when_not_to_use: Do not use the checklist as a box-ticking exercise—every 'no' answer must produce a specific action plan for the next call. A checklist is only valuable if it drives behavior change.
principle: The MEDDICC checklist is a structured diagnostic tool for evaluating the health of any deal. For Metrics: Have you quantified each pain? Are you using those numbers in the deal? For Economic Buyer: Have you identified them? Do you have agreed next steps with them? Is the deal multi-threaded? For Decision Criteria: Have you identified all evaluation criteria? Has the prospect ranked or weighted them? For Decision Process: Do you have a MAP? Have you identified a Critical Event? Have you mapped both 'getting to yes' and the paper process? For Identify Pain: Have you found at least 3 challenges? Have you uncovered business and personal impact for each? For Champion: Have you engaged at least one Champion? For Competitor: Do you know who you're competing against? Do you know the cost to the prospect of doing nothing? Every 'no' is a gap. Every gap is the next action.
recommended_action: Run the MEDDICC checklist on every active deal weekly. For every 'no' answer, write one specific action to address it in the next customer interaction. Share the checklist output in deal reviews with your sales manager to drive focused coaching. Never move a deal to the next stage in your pipeline if more than two critical checklist items are unanswered.
motm_application: Before every MOTM deal review, the BD rep should complete the MEDDICC checklist for each active opportunity. The most common MOTM gaps: Metrics (pain not quantified in ₹), Economic Buyer (not yet met the MD), Decision Process (MAP not built, paper process unknown), Champion (have a coach, not a true champion who can drive the decision internally). Each gap becomes the specific agenda item for the next customer call.

principle_name: Replace 'Just Checking In' with Purpose-Driven Follow-Up
author: Ross Keating
when_to_use: Every time you follow up with a prospect or customer after a meeting—always have a specific reason tied to the MAP and the deal's progress.
when_not_to_use: Never send 'just checking in' or 'touching base' emails—they signal that you are not in control of the deal and have no value to add.
principle: 'Just checking in' emails are a signal that the seller does not have a structured deal process and is not in control of the sales cycle. Every follow-up communication should reference the MAP, confirm or update the next agreed action, and provide a reason for the contact that is relevant to the prospect's timeline. If a deal is at risk because a MAP milestone has been missed, say so directly: 'We're now at risk of missing your January planning cycle because the decision call hasn't been confirmed.' This creates constructive urgency grounded in the prospect's own goals. All closed-ended questions, clear reasons for next steps, and MAP-referenced communications replace the passive 'touching base' approach.
questions_to_ask: As agreed, I wanted to follow up on [specific MAP item]—have you had a chance to complete that?
We're now approaching the date we agreed for [next step]—is that still on track?
Based on our MAP, the next step is [action] on [date]. Are we still aligned?
Hi [Name], I wanted to flag that we're now at risk of missing [Critical Event] if we don't confirm [next step] this week.
recommended_action: After every customer interaction, send a follow-up that references the MAP, confirms the next step, its owner, and its date. When a prospect goes silent, send a purposeful follow-up that names the specific MAP milestone at risk and its business consequence—not a passive 'checking in' message. Use the MAP as the backbone of every communication.
motm_application: Instead of: 'Hi MD, just checking in on where you are with the MOTM proposal.' Use: 'Hi MD, following up on our MAP—the CFO review was scheduled for October 17th. If that hasn't happened yet, we're now at risk of missing the November 1st agreement date, which would push the kickoff past December and into your Q1 planning window. Can we confirm where things stand?' This is specific, MAP-referenced, and creates urgency grounded in the prospect's own timeline.
